analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to share repair parts, tools, and manuals with the military at fair prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced September 4, 2025 with five cosponsors from both parties and referred to the House Armed Services Committee, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says the Pentagon cannot sign a purchase contract unless the maker agrees, in writing, to let the government and its repair contractors get the parts, tools, and repair information needed to fix the equipment. Makers would have to offer those items at the same prices and terms they give their own authorized repair shops. Existing programs could get a waiver if officials document the risks, and the Government Accountability Office would report a year after passage on how the Pentagon is complying. The Defense Secretary would also have to review existing contracts to find intellectual property restrictions that block military repairs.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would pay less for maintaining military equipment because the military would no longer have to rely on the original manufacturer as the only repair channel. Service members also benefit, since equipment repaired faster and more cheaply means higher readiness. Independent repair and maintenance firms would gain new business competing against manufacturers' authorized shops.

how_it_helps.text: No new Defense procurement contract could be signed unless the contractor agrees in writing to give the Department of Defense fair and reasonable access to all repair materials, including parts, tools, and information used to diagnose, maintain, or repair the goods.

Repair parts, tools, and information would have to be offered at prices and terms equivalent to the most favorable deal the manufacturer gives its own authorized repair providers, or, if the manufacturer offers nothing to anyone, at prices the government independently judges fair.

The Defense Secretary must review existing contracts to identify intellectual property constraints that limit the military's ability to maintain equipment and to access repair parts, tools, and information.
Within one year of enactment, the Comptroller General must report to Congress on implementation and the Defense Department's compliance with the new repair-access requirement.

analysis.who_pays: Original equipment manufacturers of military hardware would give up their lock on repair work. They would have to sell genuine parts, service tools, and repair information to the military and authorized contractors at the same terms they give their own networks, ending a stream of above-market maintenance revenue. Some manufacturers might raise initial equipment prices to make up for it.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers argue that sharing proprietary repair tools and information can raise upfront contract prices, expose intellectual property, and create security or warranty and liability concerns that the bill does not address beyond a general fairness standard.

The waiver process for pre-existing programs requires an independent technical risk assessment and justification to Congress, which adds paperwork and could leave long-running programs locked into manufacturer-only repair for years.
The bill covers only Defense Department purchases, so consumers and businesses buying similar digital equipment outside the military would get no new repair rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, well-documented problem: defense contractors using parts pairing, software locks, and repair-information restrictions to make the military dependent on them for maintenance. The potential savings are real, and the waiver process plus a GAO oversight report are reasonable guardrails against disrupting legacy programs. The main honest cost is the risk that manufacturers raise upfront prices to recover lost maintenance revenue, which the bill's fairness pricing rules only partially offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2025 and referred to the House Armed Services Committee, where it has been waiting without any committee action or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 4, 2025 by Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, joined by Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia and Rep. Maggie Goodlander, and referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.
Five cosponsors have signed on: three House Democrats and two House Republicans, giving the bill backing from both parties.
No further action has been taken since the referral; the bill has not had a committee vote, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Manufacturers of military equipment continue to hold exclusive repair rights over their products as long as the bill sits without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill's backers so far span both parties: three of 217 House Democrats and two of 223 House Republicans are cosponsors, and no one has opposed it on the record.

industries.note: Manufacturers that use parts pairing, software locks, and restricted repair information to keep the Pentagon dependent on their authorized repair networks would have to share parts, tools, and manuals at prices no worse than they give their own shops. That ends a monopoly on high-margin maintenance work, which is why the bill requires a written repair-access agreement in every new procurement contract.

industries.industry: Independent repair and defense maintenance contractors
industries.note: Non-manufacturer repair firms would finally be able to get the parts, tools, and information needed to compete for military maintenance work, and the Defense Secretary's contract-modification review would chip away at intellectual property limits that currently lock them out.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship but only five cosponsors and has sat in the House Armed Services Committee since early September with no scheduled action. Right-to-repair provisions have sometimes been attached to the annual defense authorization bill, which is the most realistic path; as a standalone bill, its likely fate is to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless the committee folds it into that larger must-pass legislation.
